title: AlphaGeometry: Olympiad Geometry Without Human Demonstrations
hook: Pair a language model with a symbolic deduction engine, train on millions of synthetic proofs, and you get a system that solves Olympiad geometry near gold-medalist level.
key_points: Combines an LM that proposes geometric constructions with a symbolic engine that verifies deduction steps.
Trained on 100 million synthetic geometry theorems and proofs - no human-labeled olympiad data needed.
Solved 25 of 30 IMO geometry problems from 2000-2022, near the average gold medalist's score.
Neuro-symbolic pairing lets each component do what it does best: language model for creativity, solver for rigor.
content_html: Trinh and colleagues at Google DeepMind published AlphaGeometry in Nature in January 2024. The system tackles International Mathematical Olympiad geometry problems by pairing a neural language model with a classical symbolic deduction engine, trained entirely on synthetic data.
extra_html:
How it works

The symbolic engine can close proofs mechanically but gets stuck when it lacks the right auxiliary constructions (new points or lines not mentioned in the problem). The language model fills that gap: it scans the proof state and proposes candidate constructions. If a proposed construction enables the symbolic engine to make progress, the process continues; otherwise a different construction is tried. Training data - 100 million theorem-proof pairs - was generated by sampling random geometry diagrams and using the symbolic engine to prove properties about them, creating a large corpus without any human annotation.

Why it matters

Formal mathematical reasoning has long been considered beyond neural models without heavy human guidance. AlphaGeometry shows that synthetic data generation plus a neuro-symbolic loop can close much of that gap, even reaching near gold-medalist performance on competition problems. The approach generalizes beyond geometry: generating synthetic formal data to bootstrap reasoning is a broadly applicable idea. Read the full paper in Nature for worked examples and an analysis of where the system still falls short.

related.hook: AlphaGo learned from human games. AlphaZero threw those away — one algorithm reached superhuman chess, shogi, and Go knowing only the rules and playing itself.

related.hook: Ask a big model to 'think step by step' and its math and logic scores jump. Reasoning was there all along — you just had to ask it to show its work.
